stem: A breast cancer screening program reports a mean survival of 9 years from diagnosis for screen-detected cases and 5 years for cases that presented with a lump. Screen-detected cases were diagnosed 4 years younger on average, tumor grade and growth rate were similar in both groups, and the mean age at death was the same.
oneliner: Screen-detected cancers: 9 y survival vs 5 y with lump, diagnosed 4 y younger, similar tumor growth, same age at death → why survival looks longer?
ask: Which best explains the longer survival in the screened women?

options.A: Diagnosis came earlier, so the survival clock started sooner without delaying death
options.B: Screening preferentially picks up slow-growing tumors with long preclinical phases
options.C: Screening finds tumors that would never have caused harm
options.D: Therapy given to screened women is more effective
options.E: Women who attend screening are healthier than those who do not

whyNot.B: That is **length-time bias**; here tumor **grade and growth rate are similar** in both groups
whyNot.C: That is **overdiagnosis**; the women here do die, at the same age as the others
whyNot.D: Better treatment would **postpone death**; here death occurs at the **same age**
whyNot.E: Selection of healthy volunteers would also **postpone death**, not leave it unchanged

why: Survival is measured **from the date of diagnosis**. Screening moved that date **4 years earlier** (9 − 5 = 4 years of extra 'survival'), yet the **age at death is identical**, so no one lived longer.
chain: Start of the survival clock moves back
Date of death does not change
Survival from diagnosis lengthens with no real benefit

idea.rule: Same age at death but longer survival from diagnosis = lead-time bias; judge screening by mortality, not survival time.
also: Compare disease-specific mortality between screened and unscreened groups
Any earlier diagnostic test can add lead time without changing outcome
Five-year survival rises when a cancer is detected earlier by imaging
Randomized screening trials avoid lead-time bias by comparing mortality

stem: A program screens men for prostate cancer once a year. Cancers found at screening are mostly low grade and slow growing, whereas aggressive cancers tend to present with symptoms in the months between screening rounds.
oneliner: Annual prostate screening, screen-detected tumors indolent, aggressive tumors appear between rounds → why screen-detected cases look less aggressive?
ask: Which best explains why screen-detected cancers appear less aggressive than interval cancers?

options.A: Diagnosis is moved earlier without changing the date of death
options.B: Cases and controls recall past exposures differently
options.C: Older age is linked to both screening and tumor behavior
options.D: Participants change behavior because they know they are observed
options.E: Periodic screening catches slow-growing tumors, which remain detectable for longer

whyNot.A: That is **lead-time bias**; an earlier diagnosis date does not change **which grade of tumor** is found
whyNot.B: That is **recall bias**, a feature of case-control history taking, not of screening rounds
whyNot.C: Age **confounding** is not suggested; the stem separates tumors by **detection method**
whyNot.D: That is the **Hawthorne effect**; it concerns altered behavior, not which tumors are caught

why: Slow-growing tumors have a **long preclinical detectable phase**, so a periodic test is more likely to find them. Fast-growing tumors surface as **interval cancers** between screens, so the screen-detected group looks falsely benign.
chain: Slow tumors stay screen-detectable for longer
Fast tumors appear between rounds as interval cancers
Screen-detected group seems to have a better prognosis

idea.rule: Length-time bias: a periodic screen over-samples slow, indolent disease.
also: Interval cancers are usually the more aggressive ones
It inflates apparent survival even if screening does nothing
Overdiagnosis is the extreme case, finding disease that never progresses
Mortality in a randomized trial removes it

stem: Investigators assign 600 adults with prior colon polyps to a high-fiber diet or their usual diet by coin flip and compare new polyps at 3 years. Recurrence is also affected by risk factors nobody measured, such as inherited variants.
oneliner: RCT of fiber diet vs usual diet for polyps, coin-flip assignment, unmeasured risk factors exist → main benefit of randomizing?
ask: What is the main benefit of randomization here?

options.A: It lowers the chance of a false-positive result
options.B: It lowers the chance of missing a real effect
options.C: Known and unknown risk factors are spread evenly between the arms
options.D: It prevents regression to the mean
options.E: It keeps observers unaware of the assigned group

whyNot.A: False positives (**type I error**) are set by the chosen alpha, not by randomization
whyNot.B: Missing a real effect (**type II error**) depends on sample size and variance
whyNot.D: **Regression to the mean** occurs in both arms; randomization does not abolish it
whyNot.E: That is **blinding**, a separate step from the coin flip

answer: Balances confounders, measured and unmeasured, across arms
why: Chance assignment makes the arms **alike at baseline on average**, including factors that **nobody measured**. Any difference in outcome is then attributable to the diet, so **confounding is controlled**.
chain: Each patient has the same chance of either diet
Arms end up similar at baseline
Unmeasured risk factors are shared evenly
Outcome difference is attributed to the diet

idea.rule: Randomization controls confounding, including confounders you cannot measure.
also: Matching and stratification handle only measured variables
Regression adjustment cannot adjust for unknown factors
Allocation concealment protects the randomization sequence
Large trials balance chance imbalances better than small ones

stem: In a trial of surgery versus medical therapy for angina, 20% of patients assigned to surgery decline the operation and take medication, and a few medical patients cross over to surgery. Investigators analyze every patient in the arm to which he or she was originally assigned.
oneliner: Surgery vs medicine RCT, 20% refuse surgery, some cross over, analysis by original assignment → why?
ask: Why is this analysis approach preferred?

options.A: It makes the treatment effect look larger
options.B: It preserves the balance between arms that randomization created
options.C: It removes the need for blinding
options.D: It raises power by excluding patients who did not comply
options.E: It removes the placebo effect

whyNot.A: Analysis as assigned usually **dilutes** the effect toward the null, not enlarges it
whyNot.C: Blinding guards against **observer and participant bias**, which analysis choice does not touch
whyNot.D: **Excluding noncompliers** is a per-protocol analysis and breaks the randomization
whyNot.E: The **placebo effect** is handled by a placebo and blinding, not by the analysis population

why: Patients who refuse or cross over are usually **different from those who adhere**. Dropping or regrouping them destroys the **comparability** achieved by randomization, so everyone is kept **as randomized**.
chain: Crossovers and dropouts are not random
Moving or removing them reintroduces confounding
Keeping everyone as assigned preserves the balance

idea.rule: Intention-to-treat: analyze as randomized to keep the arms comparable.
also: Per-protocol analysis can introduce selection bias
ITT tends to bias toward the null when crossover is high
As-treated analysis breaks randomization
ITT approximates real-world effectiveness more than efficacy

stem: Investigators debate a randomized trial versus a prospective cohort study to test a new antihypertensive. Outcome and follow-up are the same in both designs.
oneliner: New antihypertensive, RCT vs prospective cohort, same outcome and follow-up → main advantage of the RCT?
ask: What is the main advantage of the randomized trial?

options.A: Lower type I error rate
options.B: Lower type II error rate
options.C: Elimination of regression to the mean
options.D: Better control of confounding, including unmeasured factors
options.E: Lower cost and shorter duration

whyNot.A: The **alpha level** is chosen by the investigators in either design
whyNot.B: **Type II error** is governed by sample size and variance, not by design type
whyNot.C: **Regression to the mean** affects both arms; randomization does not remove it
whyNot.E: Randomized trials are usually **more expensive**, not cheaper

why: Random assignment balances **known and unknown confounders** between arms, which a cohort study cannot do. Error rates and regression to the mean are **not fixed by randomizing**.
chain: Cohort exposure is chosen by patients and doctors
Exposed and unexposed differ in other risk factors
Differences in outcome are attributed to the drug

idea.rule: The key gain of randomization is control of confounding; it does not change alpha, beta, or regression to the mean.
also: Observational designs can adjust only for measured confounders
Sample size, not design, sets type II error
A control group lets regression to the mean be measured
Blinding, not randomization, reduces observer bias

stem: Researchers want to know whether e-cigarette use in adolescence causes lung cancer, a rare outcome that would appear 30 years later.
oneliner: Teen vaping and lung cancer decades later, rare outcome → why not an RCT?
ask: Why is a randomized trial a poor choice for this question?

options.A: Assigning harm is unethical; the outcome is rare and late
options.B: Randomized trials have lower internal validity than observational studies
options.C: Randomization cannot control confounding
options.D: Randomized trials are especially prone to recall bias
options.E: A placebo cannot be used in a randomized trial

whyNot.B: RCTs have **higher** internal validity than observational designs
whyNot.C: Controlling confounding is the **strength** of randomization
whyNot.D: In a trial, exposure is **assigned and recorded prospectively**, so recall is not the problem
whyNot.E: Placebo use is **possible** in many trials and is not the limit here

answer: Ethical and practical limits of an RCT
why: You cannot **randomize people to a likely harm**. A **rare, long-latency outcome** would also need huge numbers followed for decades, so a **cohort or case-control** study is used instead.
chain: Outcome is rare and takes decades
Trial would be too large and too long

idea.rule: RCTs are unsuited to harmful exposures and to rare or long-latency outcomes.
also: Smoking and lung cancer was shown by cohort and case-control studies
Teratogens cannot be randomized in pregnancy
Rare diseases favor case-control designs
Surgical outcomes may be impractical to randomize when equipoise is absent

stem: In a crossover trial, 40 adults with hypertension take drug X for 6 weeks and then drug Y for 6 weeks, in random order. A 2-week period with no drug separates the two phases.
oneliner: Crossover antihypertensive trial, random order, 2-week no-drug gap between phases → purpose of the gap?
ask: What is the purpose of the 2-week gap?

options.A: To re-randomize patients between the phases
options.B: To reduce recall bias
options.C: To allow patients to be blinded
options.D: To increase the sample size
options.E: To let the first drug's effect wear off

whyNot.A: Randomization of **order** occurs once, at the start
whyNot.B: **Recall bias** concerns history taking in case-control studies, not drug effects
whyNot.C: Blinding comes from **matching placebo or identical tablets**, not from time off
whyNot.D: The gap does not add participants; it **adds time**

answer: Prevent carryover of the first drug's effect
why: Each patient receives both drugs, so any **lingering effect of the first drug** would contaminate the second. A **washout** long enough for clearance removes this **carryover effect**.
chain: Residual effect would add to the second drug
Washout lets drug clear and blood pressure return to baseline

idea.rule: A washout period prevents carryover in a crossover design.
also: Washout should span several half-lives of the drug
Crossover suits stable chronic disease only
Random order guards against period effects
Crossover is unsuitable for curative or irreversible treatments

stem: A rare, stable chronic disorder affects only 24 available patients. Investigators give each patient both treatments in random order instead of dividing them into two parallel groups.
oneliner: Rare stable chronic disease, 24 patients, both treatments in random order → why a crossover fits?
ask: Why does this design need fewer participants?

options.A: Randomization is no longer required
options.B: Carryover effects cannot occur
options.C: Each patient serves as his or her own control
options.D: Blinding is no longer required
options.E: The treatment effect is larger by design

whyNot.A: The **order** is still randomized to avoid period effects
whyNot.B: **Carryover** can occur, which is why a washout is added
whyNot.D: **Blinding** is still needed to avoid expectation bias
whyNot.E: The design does not enlarge the effect; it **reduces noise**

why: Comparing a patient with himself or herself **removes between-patient differences**. Less variance means the same power with **fewer subjects**.
chain: Variance of the difference is smaller

idea.rule: Each patient is his or her own control, so crossover trials need fewer subjects.
also: Paired t-test analysis fits matched or crossover data
Requires a stable, chronic condition
Needs washout between treatments
Self-controlled designs also reduce confounding by fixed traits

stem: A childhood cancer occurs in about 1 per 100,000 children. Researchers want to explore many prenatal exposures, including medications, infections and occupational contacts.
oneliner: Cancer 1 per 100,000 children, many prenatal exposures to explore → why choose case-control?
ask: Why is a case-control design the best fit?

options.A: It yields incidence directly
options.B: It starts from affected children, not a large cohort
options.C: It avoids recall bias
options.D: It gives the strongest evidence of temporality
options.E: It yields relative risk directly

whyNot.A: Sampling by outcome means the **population denominator is unknown**, so incidence cannot be calculated
whyNot.C: Exposure is reported **after** disease, so **recall bias** is a main weakness
whyNot.D: **Temporality** is clearest in a cohort or trial, not when exposure is looked up afterwards
whyNot.E: Only an **odds ratio** is available; it approximates RR only for rare disease

why: A cohort would need **millions of children** to accrue enough cases. A case-control study **begins with the cases**, matches controls, and can test **many exposures** for one rare outcome.
chain: A cohort would need huge numbers
Start with cases and sample controls

idea.rule: Rare outcome with many possible exposures: case-control.
also: Rare exposure with several outcomes suits a cohort
Odds ratio is the measure of association
Recall bias and selection of controls are the main weaknesses
Nested case-control studies sample controls from a cohort

stem: Researchers follow 2,000 benzene-exposed workers and 2,000 unexposed workers for 10 years and count new leukemia cases in each group.
oneliner: Exposed and unexposed workers followed 10 years for leukemia → why can this design report relative risk directly?
ask: Why can this design report relative risk directly?

options.A: Exposure is recalled after the disease is diagnosed
options.B: Cases are sampled separately from controls
options.C: Odds in a sample approximate risk
options.D: Incidence is measured in each exposure group
options.E: Randomization balances the groups

whyNot.A: Recalling exposure afterward describes a **case-control** study
whyNot.B: Separate sampling of cases and controls is **case-control**; here groups come from exposure
whyNot.C: **Odds ratio** approximation is the case-control method; here risks are counted directly
whyNot.E: Exposure here is **not assigned**; workers choose or happen to be exposed

why: People are **classified by exposure first** and followed forward, so the numbers at risk are known. **Incidence in each group** is therefore calculated, and **RR = incidence exposed ÷ incidence unexposed**.
chain: Count new cases in each group

idea.rule: Cohort: start from exposure, measure incidence, calculate relative risk.
also: Case-control: start from outcome, calculate odds ratio
Cohorts can study several outcomes from one exposure
Cohorts are inefficient for rare outcomes
Attributable risk also requires incidence data

stem: Using 1990 payroll records, researchers classify workers as asbestos-exposed or office-based, then review medical files to count cancers diagnosed between 1990 and 2020. All data already existed when the study began.
oneliner: Records from 1990 classify asbestos vs office workers, cancers counted to 2020 from files, all data already recorded → which design?
ask: Which design best describes this study?

options.A: Retrospective cohort study
options.B: Case-control study
options.C: Cross-sectional survey
options.D: Ecological study
options.E: Case series

whyNot.B: Case-control **starts from outcome**; here groups are formed by **exposure**
whyNot.C: Cross-sectional measures exposure and outcome **at one time**; here outcomes accrue over 30 years
whyNot.D: Ecological compares **populations**, whereas here workers are **individuals** with their own data
whyNot.E: A case series has **no comparison group**, but here two exposure groups are compared

why: The groups are **defined by past exposure** and followed forward to the outcomes. The fact that **records are historical** does not change the design; it is still a **cohort**.
chain: Exposure status taken from old records
Design is a cohort, not case-control

idea.rule: Direction of inquiry (exposure to outcome) defines a cohort, not whether data were collected in the past.
also: Prospective cohort: exposure measured now, outcomes in the future
Case-control: always starts from outcome status
Ambidirectional cohorts use both past records and future follow-up
Historical data do not make a study case-control

stem: A case-control study of a cancer with a prevalence of 1 in 10,000 reports an odds ratio of 4.2 for a chemical exposure. The authors state that the figure approximates the relative risk.
oneliner: Case-control, cancer prevalence 1 in 10,000, OR 4.2, authors say it approximates RR → on what basis?
ask: On what basis can the odds ratio be read as a relative risk?

options.A: Cases were matched to controls
options.B: The confidence interval excludes 1
options.C: Exposure was assigned at random
options.D: The numbers of cases and controls were equal
options.E: The outcome is rare in the population

whyNot.A: Matching handles **confounding**, not the OR-RR relation
whyNot.B: A significant CI shows **statistical significance**, not closeness of OR to RR
whyNot.C: Case-control studies **do not randomize**; exposure is recorded after the fact
whyNot.D: Case:control ratio is set by the **investigators** and does not matter here

why: With exposed cases a, exposed noncases b, unexposed cases c and unexposed noncases d: OR = (a/b)/(c/d) = ad/bc and RR = [a/(a+b)]/[c/(c+d)]. When disease is **rare**, a ≪ b and c ≪ d, so **a+b ≈ b and c+d ≈ d** and **OR ≈ RR**.
chain: OR uses odds, RR uses risks
Rare disease: cases small relative to non-cases
Denominators a+b and c+d approach b and d

idea.rule: When the outcome is rare, OR ≈ RR.
also: Common outcomes make OR overstate RR (when RR > 1)
Cohort and trial data give RR directly
Case-control studies can estimate only odds ratios
Logistic regression returns odds ratios

stem: A single-visit survey of 1,500 adults finds that those with depression report less weekly exercise than those without.
oneliner: One-time survey, depressed adults exercise less → why can it not show causation?
ask: Why can this survey not show that depression causes inactivity?

options.A: No measure of association can be calculated
options.B: The sample of 1,500 adults is too small
options.C: Exposure and outcome were measured at the same time
options.D: It measures incidence, not prevalence
options.E: Recall bias is always present

whyNot.A: Prevalence ratios or odds ratios **can** be calculated from survey data
whyNot.B: Sample size affects **precision**; no number of people fixes the missing **time order**
whyNot.D: A single time point measures **prevalence**, not incidence
whyNot.E: Even exact self-reports, taken at one visit, cannot show **which came first**

why: A cross-sectional study records **exposure and disease at the same moment**. The data give **prevalence** and an association but cannot show **which came first**; inactivity could cause depression or the reverse.
chain: Both variables measured at one time

idea.rule: Cross-sectional studies give prevalence and association, not temporality.
also: Prospective cohorts can show exposure preceding outcome
Case-control studies also face temporal ambiguity
Prevalence studies suit health-service planning
Reverse causation is a classic limitation

stem: A hospital reports 12 young men with a new form of pneumonia; 9 of them used the same vaping brand.
oneliner: 12 young men with new pneumonia, 9 used one vape brand → why no association can be concluded?
ask: Why can these data not show that the brand causes the illness?

options.A: The sample is too small to calculate a p value
options.B: There is no comparison group without the illness
options.C: Patients recall their vaping history inaccurately
options.D: Age confounds the association
options.E: The study looks backward in time

whyNot.A: Even a **large series** with no controls could not test an association
whyNot.C: Recall bias is not suggested; the missing piece is **who was not ill**
whyNot.D: Age may be relevant but the flaw is the **absence of any comparator**
whyNot.E: Looking backward is not the problem; **no control group** is

why: A case series only **describes patients who have the disease**. Without **unexposed or disease-free comparators**, we cannot tell if 9 of 12 is higher than in the general population, so it can only **generate hypotheses**.
chain: Rate of brand use in healthy people unknown
Hypothesis is generated for later study

idea.rule: No comparison group means no test of association; case series generate hypotheses.
also: Case-control studies add controls to test exposure rates
Cohort studies compare exposed and unexposed
Case reports often signal new drug reactions
Descriptive studies lack an analytic comparison

stem: Five patients at one clinic develop the same unusual rash within weeks of starting a newly marketed drug. Physicians publish a description of the five.
oneliner: Five patients, same unusual rash after new drug, published description → which design first signals this?
ask: Which design most often gives the first signal of a new, rare reaction like this?

options.A: Randomized controlled trial
options.B: Cohort study
options.C: Meta-analysis
options.D: Case report or case series
options.E: Ecological study

whyNot.A: Trials are designed **in advance** for known questions, and are too small for rare reactions
whyNot.B: A cohort needs a **hypothesis and a large follow-up**, which come after the signal
whyNot.C: A meta-analysis **pools existing studies**, and none exists yet
whyNot.E: An ecological study uses **aggregate data**, and nothing in the stem is population-level

why: An astute clinician sees an **unusual cluster** and writes it up. This **descriptive report** is the usual first alert to a new disease or rare reaction, and it prompts **controlled studies** to test the link.

idea.rule: Case reports and series are the first signal of new syndromes or rare drug reactions.
also: Early AIDS was first described as a cluster of unusual pneumonia and Kaposi sarcoma
Thalidomide birth defects were first noted clinically
Postmarketing surveillance relies on spontaneous reports
Signals are then tested in cohort or case-control studies

stem: Across 40 countries, those with higher average dietary fat intake have higher breast cancer rates. A commentator concludes that women who eat more fat are at higher risk.
oneliner: 40 countries: higher average fat intake, higher breast cancer rate, commentator infers individual risk → what is the flaw?
ask: What is the main flaw in applying this finding to individual women?

options.A: The data describe countries, not individual women
options.B: Cases recall past diet differently from controls
options.C: Survival is counted from an earlier diagnosis date
options.D: Controls were chosen from an unrepresentative group
options.E: Participants change behavior because they are observed

whyNot.B: That is **recall bias**, which needs individual cases and controls
whyNot.C: That is **lead-time bias**; no screening or survival data appear
whyNot.D: That is **selection bias** in a case-control study; no controls exist here
whyNot.E: That is the **Hawthorne effect**; no participants are observed

why: The unit of analysis is the **country**, so the data cannot show whether the **women who got cancer were the ones eating more fat**. A group-level link may not hold for individuals, which is the **ecological fallacy**.
chain: No individual exposure and outcome pairing
Group association may not apply to individuals

idea.rule: Group-level associations cannot be assumed to hold for individuals (ecological fallacy).
also: Countries with more TVs also have longer life expectancy, yet TVs do not prolong life
Neighborhood income and disease rate does not identify the individual patient's risk
Ecological studies generate hypotheses
Individual-level data are needed to test the hypothesis

stem: Using published national statistics, researchers plot cigarette sales against COPD mortality for 30 countries in one afternoon at almost no cost.
oneliner: National cigarette sales vs COPD mortality in 30 countries, one afternoon, almost free → why this design?
ask: What is the main reason for choosing this design?

options.A: It establishes that smoking causes COPD
options.B: It measures each smoker's individual risk
options.C: It controls for confounding between countries
options.D: It gives incidence among individuals
options.E: Existing aggregate data make it quick and cheap

whyNot.A: Aggregate correlations cannot **prove causation**
whyNot.B: Only **population averages** are used; individuals are not measured
whyNot.C: Countries differ in many ways, so **confounding is not controlled**
whyNot.D: Without individual data, **incidence in individuals** cannot be computed

why: Ecological studies reuse **existing population-level data**, so they are fast and inexpensive. They are best for **generating hypotheses** to be tested with individual-level designs.

idea.rule: Ecological studies are quick, cheap and hypothesis-generating.
also: Disease maps and time trends are ecological
They cannot assign risk to individuals
Confounding by country-level factors is common
Cohort and case-control studies test the hypothesis

stem: A first-in-human study of a new oral anticoagulant gives escalating doses to 30 healthy adult volunteers while measuring adverse effects and blood drug levels.
oneliner: First-in-human oral anticoagulant, 30 healthy volunteers, escalating doses, adverse effects and blood levels → which phase and purpose?
ask: Which phase is this, and what is its main purpose?

options.A: Phase 2: efficacy and side effects in patients
options.B: Phase 3: comparison with standard therapy in large samples
options.C: Phase 1: safety, dosing and pharmacokinetics
options.D: Phase 4: postmarketing surveillance
options.E: Preclinical: toxicity testing in animals

whyNot.A: Phase 2 uses **patients with the disease**, not healthy volunteers
whyNot.B: Phase 3 enrolls **hundreds to thousands** and compares with standard care
whyNot.D: Phase 4 follows the drug **after approval**; this drug is first-in-human
whyNot.E: Preclinical work uses **animals or cells**; here humans are dosed

why: Phase 1 gives a drug to a **small number of mostly healthy volunteers** to define **safety, tolerable dose and pharmacokinetics**. Efficacy is tested later in **patients**.

idea.rule: Phase 1 = small, healthy volunteers, safety/dose/PK; phase 2 = efficacy in patients; phase 3 = comparison; phase 4 = postmarketing.
also: Oncology phase 1 trials often use patients because of toxicity
Phase 2 gives preliminary efficacy and dose-ranging
Phase 3 trials support approval
Phase 4 detects rare adverse effects

stem: A drug is approved after trials enrolling 3,000 patients with no liver injury. Two years later, an injury occurring in about 1 in 20,000 users is reported.
oneliner: Drug approved after 3,000-patient trials with no liver injury; 2 years later a 1-in-20,000 injury is reported → where is such an event first detected?
ask: At which stage is such a rare adverse effect most likely first detected?

options.A: Phase 1
options.B: Phase 4 (postmarketing surveillance)
options.C: Phase 2
options.D: Phase 3
options.E: Preclinical animal testing

whyNot.A: **Phase 1** has only a few dozen volunteers
whyNot.C: **Phase 2** has too few patients to catch a 1-in-20,000 event
whyNot.D: **Phase 3**, at 3,000 patients, had only about a **14% chance** of seeing even one case
whyNot.E: Animal studies may **not predict** this human reaction and are far too small

why: With 1 case per 20,000 and 3,000 trial patients, the chance of seeing even one case is 1 − (1 − 1/20,000)^3,000 ≈ 14%. After approval, **far larger numbers and longer exposure** make **rare events** detectable.
chain: Premarketing trials enroll thousands at most
Rare event too uncommon to appear
Large numbers and long exposure reveal the event

idea.rule: Rare adverse effects typically surface in phase 4 because premarketing trials are too small and short.
also: Spontaneous reporting systems detect signals
Drug withdrawals often follow phase 4 findings
Long-latency effects need long follow-up
Rule of three: to see one event of rate 1/N with 95% confidence needs about 3N patients

stem: A meta-analysis pools 10 small industry-funded trials of a supplement and reports a significant benefit. The funnel plot is asymmetric, with the smaller studies showing larger effects.
oneliner: Meta-analysis of 10 small industry-funded trials, asymmetric funnel plot, small studies show larger effects → main limitation?
ask: What is the main limitation of the pooled estimate?

options.A: Pooling lowers power compared with any single trial
options.B: Group-level data are applied to individuals
options.C: Survival is counted from an earlier diagnosis date
options.D: Publication bias carries into the pooled result
options.E: Trial participants recall their exposures differently

whyNot.A: Pooling **increases** power, so this is not the main problem
whyNot.B: That is the **ecological fallacy**; trials here enroll individuals
whyNot.C: That is **lead-time bias** from screening, which is not suggested
whyNot.E: That is **recall bias** of case-control studies; these are trials

answer: Garbage in, garbage out: bias in included studies and publication bias
why: A meta-analysis can only be as valid as its **included studies**. An **asymmetric funnel plot** suggests **missing small negative studies** (publication bias), so the pooled benefit is likely **overstated**.

idea.rule: A meta-analysis inherits the biases of its studies, including publication bias.
also: Funnel plot asymmetry suggests publication bias
Heterogeneity (I²) should be assessed
Industry funding may bias design and reporting
Pooling trials with high risk of bias gives a precise but biased estimate

stem: A 44-year-old woman has pleuritic chest pain, and her physician judges her pretest probability of pulmonary embolism to be low. A high-sensitivity D-dimer assay, with 98% sensitivity for pulmonary embolism, is negative, and the physician stops the work-up.
oneliner: 44F + low pretest probability of PE + D-dimer sensitivity 98% + negative result → why PE is excluded?
ask: Which test property best explains why this negative result rules out pulmonary embolism?

options.A: High sensitivity
options.B: High specificity
options.C: High positive predictive value
options.D: High reliability
options.E: High positive likelihood ratio

whyNot.B: High specificity makes a **positive** result convincing (SpPin); it does not govern a negative one
whyNot.C: **PPV** describes what a positive result means, and it falls with low prevalence
whyNot.D: Reliability is **reproducibility** of repeated results; a reproducible test can still miss disease, and the stem's clue is the **98% sensitivity**
whyNot.E: **LR+** applies to positive results; the stem gives a negative one

why: With **98% sensitivity** only about 2% of diseased patients test negative, so **false negatives are rare** and a **negative result excludes disease** (SnNout). A highly specific test does the opposite job: a positive result rules disease in (SpPin).

idea.rule: Sensitive test, negative result: rules out (SnNout); specific test, positive result: rules in (SpPin).
also: Screening tests are chosen for high sensitivity
Confirmatory tests are chosen for high specificity
NPV rises with sensitivity and with low prevalence

stem: A 4-year-old boy has severe diarrhea, and the team is considering a therapy that is toxic to anyone treated needlessly, so false-positive results would be harmful. Three independent diagnostic tests are available, each with good but imperfect specificity.
oneliner: 4M + severe diarrhea + toxic therapy + three imperfect tests + false positives harmful → testing strategy?
ask: Which testing strategy best ensures that only true cases are treated?

options.A: Parallel testing, treating when any test is positive
options.B: Serial testing, treating only when all tests are positive
options.C: Treating on the single most sensitive test alone
options.D: Repeating the most sensitive test and treating if positive
options.E: Running a second test only when the first is negative

whyNot.A: Parallel testing raises **sensitivity**, so it adds false positives, the harm the team wants to avoid
whyNot.C: The most sensitive test alone, with **imperfect specificity**, still lets false positives through; it cannot confirm disease
whyNot.D: Repeating the same test does not raise specificity much; it **tends to repeat the same false positives**
whyNot.E: Testing further only after a negative result is **parallel logic**, aimed at catching missed cases

why: Requiring **every test to be positive** (serial testing) means a false positive must occur on all of them, so **specificity and PPV rise** above those of any single test. That fits a **toxic treatment** where false positives cause harm; parallel testing instead raises sensitivity and NPV.

idea.rule: Serial testing raises specificity and PPV; parallel testing raises sensitivity and NPV.
also: Serial: confirm before a risky treatment
Parallel: do not miss a dangerous disease
Combining tests changes accuracy, not prevalence

stem: A bathroom scale is checked with a volunteer whose weight is known to be 65 kg. Three consecutive readings are 70.0, 70.1 and 70.0 kg.
oneliner: Scale readings 70.0, 70.1, 70.0 kg vs true 65 kg → what property is lacking?
ask: Which best describes the scale and the type of error responsible?

options.A: Precise and accurate, with little error
options.B: Accurate but imprecise, from random error
options.C: Precise but inaccurate, from systematic error
options.D: Imprecise and inaccurate, from random error
options.E: Precise but inaccurate, from random error

whyNot.A: Readings cluster tightly but **sit about 5 kg above the true 65 kg**, so the scale is not accurate
whyNot.B: The readings are **about 5 kg off** the true weight, so it is not accurate, and they agree within 0.1 kg, so it is not imprecise
whyNot.D: The three readings **differ by only 0.1 kg**, so random error is small and the scale is not imprecise
whyNot.E: Random error would scatter the readings; here **every reading is shifted by the same ~5 kg**, a systematic error

why: The readings agree within 0.1 kg, so the scale is **precise** (reproducible, little random error). All are about **5 kg too high**, a consistent offset, so it is **inaccurate** because of **systematic error** (miscalibration).

idea.rule: Precision is reproducibility (hurt by random error); accuracy is closeness to truth (hurt by systematic error).
also: Averaging more readings improves precision, not accuracy
Recalibration fixes systematic error
Wide scatter of repeat readings means poor precision

stem: A registry finds that a chronic disease has the same yearly incidence in women and men, yet its prevalence is 3 times higher in women.
oneliner: Equal incidence + prevalence 3 times higher in one sex → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains the higher prevalence in women?

options.A: Higher case fatality in women
options.B: More new cases in women
options.C: Shorter disease course in women
options.D: Longer disease course in women
options.E: More uncounted mild cases in men

whyNot.A: Higher fatality **shortens duration** and would lower prevalence in women
whyNot.B: Incidence (new cases) is **equal** in the two groups by the stem
whyNot.C: A shorter course would **lower** prevalence in women, not raise it
whyNot.E: Uncounted cases in men would lower **both** measured incidence and prevalence in men, but the stem gives **equal incidence**

answer: Longer disease duration in women (about 3 times)
why: **Prevalence = incidence × mean duration.** With **equal incidence**, a prevalence 3 times higher means **duration is about 3 times longer**, from slower cure or longer survival.
chain: Duration must be longer in women

idea.rule: Prevalence = incidence × duration, so at equal incidence a higher prevalence means longer illness.
also: A new treatment that prolongs life without curing raises prevalence
A faster cure lowers prevalence at constant incidence
A short, fatal illness has low prevalence even if common at onset

stem: A case-control study of occupational solvent exposure and bladder cancer reports an odds ratio of 2.4, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.3 to 4.4.
oneliner: Case-control, OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.3-4.4 → correct interpretation?
ask: Which statement is the correct interpretation of this interval?

options.A: There is a 95% probability the true OR is exactly 2.4
options.B: 95% of exposed workers have an OR between 1.3 and 4.4
options.C: The result is not significant because the interval is wide
options.D: The association is significant, with a p value of about 0.95
options.E: 95% of intervals from repeated studies would hold the true OR

whyNot.A: A single **point estimate** has no 95% probability of being exactly right
whyNot.B: The odds ratio belongs to the **group comparison**, not to individual workers
whyNot.C: The interval **excludes 1.0**, so the result is significant; width reflects only precision
whyNot.D: A 95% CI that excludes 1.0 corresponds to **p < 0.05**, not 0.95

answer: About 95% of such intervals from repeated samples would contain the true OR
why: The **95% confidence level** describes the method: across **repeated samples**, 95% of intervals built this way contain the true value. Because **1.0 lies outside 1.3 to 4.4**, the association is statistically significant (p < 0.05).
chain: Interval comes from a method that captures the truth 95% of the time
Not a probability about one number

idea.rule: A 95% CI describes repeated-sampling coverage; if it excludes the null value, p < 0.05.
also: For a ratio, the null value is 1.0
For a difference, the null value is 0
A wider interval means less precision

stem: A study measures fasting glucose in 25 adults and finds a mean of 130 mg/dL with a standard deviation of 25 mg/dL. The investigators calculate the 95% confidence interval for the mean.
oneliner: n 25, glucose mean 130, SD 25 → why CI uses SE, not SD?
ask: Why is the confidence interval for the mean built from the standard error rather than the standard deviation?

options.A: SE reflects uncertainty in the mean, not individual spread
options.B: SD is always the larger of the two numbers
options.C: SD shrinks steadily as the sample size grows
options.D: SE describes the variation among individuals
options.E: SE equals SD once the sample exceeds 30

whyNot.B: Size is not the reason; the two answer **different questions**
whyNot.C: SD does not shrink systematically with n; it is **SE (SD/√n)** that does
whyNot.D: That is the **SD**; SE tells how far the sample mean may be from the true mean
whyNot.E: SE = SD/√n, so it is **always smaller** than SD for n > 1 (here 5 vs 25)

answer: SE reflects uncertainty in the mean; SD reflects spread of individuals
why: A CI quantifies how well the sample **mean** estimates the population mean, which is the job of the **SE = SD/√n** = 25/√25 = 5. The 95% CI is 130 ± 1.96 × 5 = **120.2 to 139.8 mg/dL**; the SD describes individual scatter.
chain: SE describes uncertainty of the mean

idea.rule: SD describes individuals; SE (SD/√n) describes the precision of the mean and builds the CI.
also: Bigger n gives smaller SE
SD does not fall as n rises
About 95% of individuals lie within mean ± 2 SD (normal data)

stem: Leukocyte counts in healthy adults follow a symmetric, bell-shaped normal distribution with a mean of 7,500 cells/µL.
oneliner: WBC normally distributed, mean 7,500 → percent above the mean?
ask: What percentage of healthy adults have counts above the mean, and why?

options.A: About 68%, because that share lies within 1 SD
options.B: About 50%, because mean, median and mode coincide
options.C: About 95%, because that share lies within 2 SD
options.D: Under 50%, because the mean exceeds the median
options.E: Over 50%, because the mode exceeds the mean

whyNot.A: 68% is the share **within** ±1 SD, not the share above the mean
whyNot.C: 95% is the share within ±2 SD of the mean, not above it
whyNot.D: In a **symmetric** curve the mean does **not** exceed the median
whyNot.E: In a symmetric curve the mode **equals** the mean

why: In a normal distribution the **mean, median and mode coincide** at the centre, and the curve is **symmetric**, so half the values lie above the mean and half below.

idea.rule: Normal distribution: symmetric, mean = median = mode, 50% on each side.
also: 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD
Positive skew: mean > median > mode
Negative skew: mean < median < mode

stem: An observational study of 500 adults finds a correlation coefficient of r = 0.6 between serum LDL cholesterol and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein.
oneliner: 500 adults + observational + LDL vs hs-CRP r = 0.6 → what can be concluded?
ask: Which conclusion is supported by this finding?

options.A: Higher LDL causes higher CRP
options.B: Higher CRP causes higher LDL
options.C: Higher LDL goes with higher CRP
options.D: 60% of high-LDL adults have high CRP
options.E: LDL and CRP are not related

whyNot.A: Observational correlation alone **cannot establish causation**
whyNot.B: Likewise **cannot show** that CRP drives LDL; direction is unknown
whyNot.D: r is the **strength of a linear association**, not a percentage of people
whyNot.E: r = 0.6 is a **moderate positive** association, so a relationship exists

answer: Positive association only; no cause or direction
why: **r = 0.6** shows the values move together (positive, moderate), but correlation reflects **association only**; it does not show **causation or direction**, and a third factor could drive both.

idea.rule: Correlation measures strength and sign of association only, never causation.
also: r ranges from -1 to +1
r² is the share of variance explained
r = 0 means no linear association

stem: A researcher surveys dietary habits by approaching whoever walks into a single health-food store over two weeks. Recruitment is quick and cheap, and participants are not randomly chosen.
oneliner: Diet survey of whoever enters one health-food store, non-random → main drawback?
ask: Which of the following is the main drawback of this sampling method?

options.A: Recall bias
options.B: Lead-time bias
options.C: Confounding
options.D: Selection bias
options.E: Observer bias

whyNot.A: Recall bias comes from **memory of past exposure** differing by group, not from how people are recruited
whyNot.B: Lead-time bias arises in **screening** studies, by earlier diagnosis
whyNot.C: Confounding concerns a **third factor** linked to exposure and outcome, not who is sampled
whyNot.E: Observer bias arises from the **rater's expectations** during measurement

why: A **convenience sample** is fast and cheap but not random, so participants (health-food shoppers) may **not represent the target population**. The main drawback is **selection bias**, which limits external validity.
chain: Shoppers differ from the general population

idea.rule: Non-random sampling risks selection bias, because the sample may not represent the target population.
also: Random sampling reduces selection bias
Volunteers differ from non-volunteers
Loss to follow-up also causes selection bias

stem: A cohort study follows employees of a chemical plant and finds that their all-cause mortality is lower than that of the general population. The comparison group is the general public.
oneliner: Chemical plant workers' mortality lower than public's → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains this finding?

options.A: The chemical exposure protects against death
options.B: Workers recalled their exposures better
options.C: Disease was detected earlier by screening
options.D: Workers behaved better while being watched
options.E: Healthier people are the ones who stay employed

whyNot.A: Protection is implausible; lower all-cause mortality arises from the **choice of the general public as comparison**
whyNot.B: Recall of exposure matters in **case-control** studies; this cohort compares mortality, not recalled exposure
whyNot.C: Earlier detection is **lead-time bias**; the stem describes no screening
whyNot.D: That is the **Hawthorne effect**; nothing in the stem says workers knew they were watched

why: Only people healthy enough to work are employed, so a workforce is **healthier than the general population**, which includes the ill and disabled. This **healthy worker effect** biases occupational cohorts toward **understating risk**.

idea.rule: Healthy worker effect: employed people are healthier than the public, so occupational risk is understated.
also: Compare with other workers instead of the public
It is a form of selection bias
It hides true occupational hazards

stem: In a case-control study, mothers of infants born with birth defects report more medication use during pregnancy than mothers of healthy infants. Exposure was obtained from self-report after delivery.
oneliner: Case-control + self-reported past exposure, case mothers report more → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains the difference in reported exposure?

options.A: Recall bias
options.B: Selection bias
options.C: Lead-time bias
options.D: Confounding
options.E: Observer bias

whyNot.B: Selection bias concerns **who enters the study**, not how exposure is reported
whyNot.C: Lead-time bias arises when **screening** advances diagnosis
whyNot.D: Confounding needs a **third factor** tied to both exposure and outcome; none is given
whyNot.E: Observer bias is from the **interviewer's** expectations, not the mothers' memory

why: Mothers of affected infants **search their memory harder** for possible causes than control mothers, so reported exposure is **inflated in cases**. This **recall bias** is typical of **case-control** studies relying on self-reported past exposure.

idea.rule: Recall bias: cases remember or report past exposures differently from controls, distorting case-control results.
also: Use medical records to confirm exposure
Cohort studies avoid it by measuring exposure first
Affects exposure data from self-report

stem: A survey finds that people who carry matches in their pockets have a higher rate of lung cancer. Carrying matches does not cause lung cancer, but smokers carry matches and smoking causes lung cancer.
oneliner: Matches in pocket linked to lung cancer + smokers carry matches → why crude association misleading?
ask: Which of the following best explains the crude association?

options.A: Effect modification
options.B: Confounding
options.C: Recall bias
options.D: Reverse causation
options.E: Selection bias

whyNot.A: Effect modification means the **effect itself differs** across levels of a third variable
whyNot.C: Recall bias comes from **unequal memory** of exposures, which is not described
whyNot.D: Cancer does not cause people to carry matches; **smoking drives both**
whyNot.E: Nothing in the stem describes **how subjects were selected**

why: **Smoking** is associated with both the exposure (carrying matches) and the outcome (lung cancer) and is not on a causal path between them. It creates a **false association**, which is **confounding**.

idea.rule: A confounder is linked to both exposure and outcome, is not on the causal path, and creates a false association.
also: Control by stratification or multivariable adjustment
Randomization balances confounders
Matching also controls them

stem: In a randomized trial of a new drug, 30% of participants in the drug arm drop out because of side effects, compared with 5% in the placebo arm. Analysis includes only those who finish.
oneliner: RCT, dropout 30% drug arm vs 5% placebo arm → which validity is threatened?
ask: Which type of validity is most directly threatened?

options.A: External validity
options.B: Reliability
options.C: Internal validity
options.D: Precision
options.E: Face validity

whyNot.A: External validity concerns **applying results to other populations**, not bias within the trial
whyNot.B: Reliability is **reproducibility** of a measurement, not bias from dropout
whyNot.D: Precision relates to **random error** and sample size
whyNot.E: Face validity is whether a **measurement tool appears** to assess what it intends, not bias from losing participants

why: **Unequal loss to follow-up** leaves the groups no longer comparable, producing **bias** in the studied sample. Truth for the people studied is **internal validity**, and it is a prerequisite for external validity.

idea.rule: Internal validity is whether the result is true for the people studied, free of bias and confounding.
also: Intention-to-treat analysis protects it
External validity requires internal validity
Differential dropout is a form of selection bias

stem: Hospital staff wash their hands much more often during the week an infection-control team openly observes the ward, and return to old habits after the team leaves.
oneliner: Staff wash hands more when infection-control team watches → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains the improvement?

options.A: Placebo effect
options.B: Pygmalion effect
options.C: Regression to the mean
options.D: Hawthorne effect
options.E: Recall bias

whyNot.A: The placebo effect is improvement from **expecting benefit of an inert treatment**; none is given
whyNot.B: The Pygmalion effect is **performance rising with the observer's high expectations**, not from being watched
whyNot.C: Regression to the mean applies to **extreme measurements** drifting back, not behavior tied to observation
whyNot.E: Recall bias concerns **memory of past exposure**, whereas this behavior is directly observed

why: Subjects **change their behavior because they know they are being observed**. Hand washing rises while the team watches and **falls when observation ends**, the **Hawthorne effect**.

idea.rule: Hawthorne effect: people alter behavior simply because they know they are being observed.
also: An equally observed control group helps account for it
Covert observation avoids it
It threatens the validity of behavioral studies

stem: In an open-label, single-arm trial of a new pill for migraine, 40% of participants report fewer headaches. The outcome is a self-reported symptom score, and there is no control group.
oneliner: Open-label single-arm migraine trial, 40% improve, subjective outcome → why add placebo arm?
ask: Why does this trial need a blinded placebo arm?

options.A: To eliminate recall bias in symptom reports
options.B: To make the results apply to more patients
options.C: To remove lead-time bias from early diagnosis
options.D: To let participants switch to the other arm
options.E: To tell drug effect from expectation or natural course

whyNot.A: Recall bias comes from **memory of past exposure** and is not fixed by a placebo
whyNot.B: Applicability (external validity) depends on **who is enrolled**, not on a control arm
whyNot.C: Lead-time bias belongs to **screening** studies; no screening is described
whyNot.D: Switching arms is a **crossover design**; the stem's problem is that there is **no comparison group**

answer: A blinded placebo arm isolates the drug effect
why: With a **subjective outcome** and **no control group**, improvement may reflect **expectation (placebo effect)** or the **natural course** of migraine. A **blinded placebo arm** lets the drug's true effect be estimated as the difference between arms.
chain: Improvement from expectation or natural course

idea.rule: A blinded placebo control separates drug effect from expectation and natural course.
also: Double-blinding reduces observer bias
Regression to the mean also inflates uncontrolled results
Placebo response is common with subjective outcomes

stem: Investigators compare mean LDL cholesterol (a continuous outcome) among participants assigned to three different diets.
oneliner: Mean LDL (continuous) across 3 diet groups → which test?
ask: Which statistical test is most appropriate?

options.A: ANOVA
options.B: Two-sample t-test
options.C: Chi-square test
options.D: Pearson correlation
options.E: Paired t-test

whyNot.B: A t-test compares **only two** means; repeated t-tests would inflate type I error
whyNot.C: Chi-square compares **proportions** of a categorical outcome, but LDL is continuous
whyNot.D: Correlation measures **association of two continuous variables**, not group differences
whyNot.E: A paired t-test is for **two measurements on the same subjects**; groups here are separate and number three

why: A **continuous outcome** compared across **three groups** calls for **ANOVA**. Doing several t-tests would **inflate the type I error**, so one test compares all the means together.
chain: Compare means of 3 or more groups

idea.rule: Means of 3 or more groups: ANOVA; repeated t-tests inflate type I error.
also: Two means: t-test
Proportions: chi-square
Two continuous variables: correlation or regression

stem: A study compares the percentage of smokers and nonsmokers who develop a chronic cough, using counts of people with and without cough in each group.
oneliner: % smokers vs nonsmokers with cough (categorical, counts) → which test?
ask: Which statistical test is most appropriate?

options.A: Two-sample t-test
options.B: Chi-square test
options.C: ANOVA
options.D: Pearson correlation
options.E: Paired t-test

whyNot.A: A t-test compares **means** of a continuous variable, but the outcome here is yes or no
whyNot.C: ANOVA compares **means among 3 or more** groups; this is a categorical outcome in two groups
whyNot.D: Correlation relates **two continuous variables**; counts are categorical
whyNot.E: A paired t-test needs **matched continuous measures**; the groups are independent

why: The outcome (cough or no cough) is **categorical**, summarized as **counts** in two groups. Comparing proportions between groups uses the **chi-square test**.

idea.rule: Categorical outcome across groups (proportions): chi-square test.
also: Fisher exact test for small expected counts
Continuous outcome: t-test or ANOVA
Chi-square can compare more than two groups

stem: A 62-year-old French-speaking woman is scheduled for surgery and needs to give informed consent. Her bilingual daughter offers to interpret, but the hospital has a professional interpreter service.
oneliner: 62F + French-speaking + surgery consent + daughter offers to interpret → best approach?
ask: What is the most appropriate approach to consent?

options.A: Let the daughter interpret, since family is faster
options.B: Use gestures and pictures to avoid translation errors
options.C: Use a professional medical interpreter for consent
options.D: Have the daughter sign the consent on her behalf
options.E: Ask a French-speaking clerk from the front office

whyNot.A: Speed does not matter if the daughter **mistranslates or filters** risks and undermines consent
whyNot.B: Gestures **cannot convey** the risks, benefits and alternatives of surgery
whyNot.D: The patient is the one consenting; a relative signs only if the patient **lacks capacity**, which the stem does not suggest
whyNot.E: An untrained employee has the **same risk of error**; a trained interpreter is available

why: A **professional interpreter** is trained in medical terms and neutrality. A relative may **mistranslate or omit medical or cultural details**, or filter information, which **threatens informed consent and safety**.

idea.rule: Use a trained medical interpreter, not family, for consent and medical discussions.
also: Children should not interpret
Speak to the patient, not the interpreter
Document the interpreter used

stem: A 48-year-old woman has waited 30 minutes in the clinic because the physician was delayed by an emergency. As the physician enters, the patient looks at her watch and appears irritated.
oneliner: 48F + waited 30 min, physician delayed by emergency + patient irritated → best opening statement?
ask: Which opening statement by the physician is most appropriate?

options.A: "An emergency came up, so the delay really was not my fault."
options.B: "Sorry for the delay; this visit will be very quick, I promise."
options.C: "Sorry I'm late; would you prefer to reschedule for another day?"
options.D: "I'm sorry to have kept you waiting; I know your time is valuable."
options.E: "Sorry I'm late; the front desk overbooked my schedule again today."

whyNot.A: Explaining first **defends the physician** and skips acknowledging her irritation
whyNot.B: Promising speed may be **untrue** and rushes a patient who has already waited
whyNot.C: Offering to reschedule **sends her away** after she waited 30 minutes, without empathy
whyNot.E: Blaming staff **shifts responsibility** (and the delay was an emergency), which erodes trust

why: The patient's **inconvenience is real** even though the delay was unavoidable. A brief **apology with an empathic statement** acknowledges her time and rebuilds trust; an explanation can follow.
chain: Delay was not the physician's fault

idea.rule: Apologize with empathy for a patient's inconvenience, even when the delay was not your fault.
also: Do not blame colleagues
Avoid defensive explanations first
Empathy builds the therapeutic relationship

stem: A 56-year-old man in the emergency department says his own physician is arrogant and never returns his phone calls. He asks what the ED physician thinks.
oneliner: 56M + ED + complains own physician arrogant, never calls back → best response?
ask: Which response by the ED physician is most appropriate?

options.A: Offer to call his physician about the complaint
options.B: Tell him to report his physician to the licensing board
options.C: Reassure him that such behavior is common among doctors
options.D: Give him a printed copy of the patient bill of rights
options.E: Encourage him to tell his own physician his concerns

whyNot.A: Contacting the physician for him **bypasses the patient** and involves a third party
whyNot.B: Reporting to a board is **disproportionate** for poor communication
whyNot.C: Calling the behavior common **dismisses** and invalidates his concerns
whyNot.D: A document does not **address his concern** or repair the relationship

why: The complaint is about **communication**, which the patient can best fix with his own doctor. Encouraging him to **speak to his physician directly** validates his concerns and strengthens that relationship without involving third parties.

idea.rule: A dissatisfied patient should be encouraged to speak directly to his physician about the concern.
also: Do not criticize a colleague
Escalate only for serious misconduct
Listen without taking sides

stem: A 60-year-old woman must choose between two reasonable treatments for her condition. After the options are explained, she asks, "What would you do?"
oneliner: 60F + choosing between two treatments + asks 'What would you do?' → best response?
ask: Which response by the physician is most appropriate?

options.A: Ask what she understands and what matters most to her
options.B: Tell her that the decision is hers alone to make
options.C: Recommend the option the physician would personally choose
options.D: Refer her to a colleague for a second opinion
options.E: Repeat the statistics on both options and let her decide

whyNot.B: Withdrawing leaves her **without guidance** when she has asked for it
whyNot.C: The physician's own values may **differ from hers**; they must be learned first
whyNot.D: Referral **avoids** the question she asked
whyNot.E: The options were **already explained**; repeating numbers does not answer her or learn her values

why: When asked for advice, **first explore what the patient understands and values** about the options. This lets the physician give a recommendation that **fits her preferences** while keeping the decision shared.

idea.rule: When a patient asks for advice, first explore her understanding and values, then recommend.
also: Shared decision-making respects autonomy
Do not impose the physician's values
Use open-ended questions
